article_title: UC Berkeley's 48-Sensor Computational Microscope Captures 25.2 Billion Pixels Per Second, Tracks Live C. elegans
summary: Automated checks passed, but Chief Editor overrides to REJECT: this submission is a duplicate of the article already published minutes earlier from PR #2117 (same UC Berkeley/Nature Photonics computational microscope study, same 25.2 billion px/s figure, same quotes, same C. elegans demo, 2 of 3 identical sources), and separately contains a fabricated source attribution and a false claim about source inaccessibility.

findings.message: Source fetched via Archive.org fallback (original returned 200)

findings.details: PR #2117 ("UC Berkeley's Computational Microscope Captures 25.2 Billion Pixels Per Second Across a Wide Field of View") was merged and published at src/content/articles/2026-08/04-uc-berkeleys-computational-microscope-captures-252-billion-pixels-per-second-across-a-wide-field-of-view.md minutes before this PR was opened. Both cover the identical Nature Photonics study (Zhou, Gu, Waller et al., UC Berkeley), the identical 25.2 billion pixels/second and 3-micron/5cm^2/120fps figures, the identical phase-mask/48-sensor mechanism, and the identical C. elegans pharyngeal-pumping demonstration, sourced from the same UC Berkeley engineering release and the same Phys.org syndication (2 of this submission's 3 sources are identical URLs to the published article's 2 sources). This submission adds a third source (the Nature Photonics DOI page) and reformats the same facts/quotes as bullet points plus an added 'Analysis' paragraph, but offers no new facts, no new development, and no materially different angle.

findings.message: Quote fabricated / not verbatim in cited source
findings.details: Body text attributes the quoted fragment "a computational algorithm then reconstructs the complete image from this compressed data" to Phys.org (https://phys.org/news/2026-08-focus-microscope-captures-billion-pixels.html). This exact phrase does not appear anywhere in the Phys.org snapshot (sources/2026-08/.../source-1.html.gz, sha256 4769a7f7...). The closest Phys.org text is Waller's verbatim quote "...we were able to fill in the data gaps and reconstruct the image," which is materially different wording. The adjacent quoted fragment "redirects light that would normally fall between the sensors" is also not verbatim in Phys.org, which instead reads "light that would normally fall between the sensors is redirected onto them instead."

The 'What We Don't Know' section states the Nature Photonics paper's page "returned an authentication redirect rather than article text." The source-2 snapshot (sources/2026-08/.../source-2.html.gz, sha256 f9ec9024...) shows the article is explicitly labeled "Article Open access" and the full abstract and 'Main' body text (introduction, methods) are present in the snapshot with no paywall, login wall, or subscription prompt anywhere in the extracted text. The claim that the paper was inaccessible is factually false relative to the very snapshot the bot's own pipeline fetched.

content_preview.title: UC Berkeley's 48-Sensor Computational Microscope Captures 25.2 Billion Pixels Per Second, Tracks Live C. elegans
content_preview.summary: A UC Berkeley-led team built a computational microscope combining 48 sensors and a diffractive phase mask to hit 25.2 billion pixels per second.
content_preview.body_excerpt:
## Overview

A UC Berkeley-led team of researchers has built a computational microscope that captures 25.2 billion pixels per second, achieving 3-micron resolution across 5 square centimeters at 120 frames per second, according to [UC Berkeley College of Engineering](https://engineering.berkeley.edu/news/2026/07/bringing-it-all-into-focus/). The device, described in a study published in Nature Photonics, is designed to sidestep a long-standing trade-off in microscope design between imaging speed...

editor_notes.content_quality: The submission is well-written, correctly formatted, and its automated checks all pass. On a standalone basis the prose is neutral and the sourcing structure is sound. However two specific integrity problems were found on manual review: (1) a quoted fragment attributed to Phys.org ('a computational algorithm then reconstructs the complete image from this compressed data') does not appear verbatim, or in substance, anywhere in the Phys.org snapshot; (2) the 'What We Don't Know' section falsely claims the Nature Photonics paper's page 'returned an authentication redirect rather than article text,' when the source-2 snapshot is explicitly labeled 'Article Open access' and contains the full abstract and body text with no paywall or login wall present.
editor_notes.source_verification: Read all three snapshots in sources/2026-08/uc-berkeleys-48-sensor-computational-microscope-captures-252-billion-pixels-per-second-tracks-live-c-elegans/ after verifying each file's sha256 against manifest.json (all three matched). source-0.html.gz (UC Berkeley College of Engineering, engineering.berkeley.edu) fully supports the article's core facts and every direct quote attributed to it (Waller x4, Zhou x1, Gu x1) appears verbatim. source-1.html.gz (Phys.org, fetched via Archive.org fallback per manifest, live URL still returned 200) is substantially a syndication of the same UC Berkeley release and supports most claims, but does NOT contain the quoted fragment 'a computational algorithm then reconstructs the complete image from this compressed data' attributed to it in the body — this is a fabricated/hallucinated quote. source-2.html.gz (Nature Photonics, nature.com) is an open-access article and its abstract and Main/introduction body text are fully present in the snapshot; the submission's claim that this page was inaccessible behind an authentication redirect is false. manifest.json shows suspicious_patterns: null for all three sources — no prompt-injection content found in any snapshot.
editor_notes.factual_accuracy: Every numeric specific checked against the UC Berkeley snapshot (25.2 billion pixels/second, 3-micron resolution, 5 square centimeters, 120 fps, 48 sensors, 15-second C. elegans demo, collaborator list, funding list) is accurate and correctly attributed. The two issues found are not about the underlying facts being wrong, but about (a) a quote fabricated in the body text and misattributed to a specific outlet, and (b) a fabricated excuse for why a source supposedly could not be used, when the pipeline's own snapshot shows it was fully readable.
editor_notes.tone_assessment: Neutral and professional; no sensationalism or AI self-reference observed.
editor_notes.originality: REJECT-triggering. PR #2117 ('UC Berkeley's Computational Microscope Captures 25.2 Billion Pixels Per Second Across a Wide Field of View') was reviewed, approved, merged, and published to src/content/articles/2026-08/04-uc-berkeleys-computational-microscope-captures-252-billion-pixels-per-second-across-a-wide-field-of-view.md only minutes before this PR (#2118) was opened, per git log (33d3c73ba Review: APPROVE, 7b0a45a1f Merge, 45ae2a207 Publish, all dated 2026-08-04, versus this submission's 2026-08-04T08:43:53Z timestamp). I read the full published article body. Both articles: cover the exact same Nature Photonics paper (Zhou, Gu, Ikeda, Hayward, Antipa, Menon, Horstmeyer, Kato, Waller); report the identical headline figure (25.2 billion pixels/second) and identical resolution/FOV/frame-rate figures (3-micron, 5cm^2, 120fps); describe the identical 48-sensor array and phase-mask mechanism; quote the same Waller 'breakthrough' and 'space-bandwidth time product' lines, the same Zhou C. elegans/pharyngeal-pumping quote, and the same Gu calibration-free quote; and cite 2 of 3 identical source URLs (engineering.berkeley.edu and phys.org — the only new source in this submission is the Nature Photonics DOI page itself, which the submission's own body claims -- falsely -- it could not read). The only differences are cosmetic: bullet-point structure vs. prose, and an added 'Analysis' paragraph that restates the same computational-imaging framing already present in the published article's Waller quotes, without introducing any new fact, statistic, expert reaction, or development. This is a duplicate of already-published coverage with no new information or angle, meeting the Step 5 REJECT criteria exactly ('The exact same story was already published' / 'essentially a rewrite of an existing article').
concerns: Duplicate of already-published article (PR #2117 / src/content/articles/2026-08/04-uc-berkeleys-computational-microscope-captures-252-billion-pixels-per-second-across-a-wide-field-of-view.md) covering the identical study, identical figures, identical quotes, with no new facts or angle.
Fabricated quote attributed to Phys.org ('a computational algorithm then reconstructs the complete image from this compressed data') not present in the source-1 snapshot.

False claim in 'What We Don't Know' that the Nature Photonics source page was inaccessible behind an authentication redirect, when the source-2 snapshot shows an open-access article with full text present.
recommendations: REJECT. Not eligible for a corrections-note fix: the duplication is a wholesale story overlap (not a single recoverable specific), and it is compounded by two independent fabrication issues (a misattributed quote and a false inaccessibility claim) that constitute a pattern, not a single slip. Per the v3.9.0 workflow this submission is discarded; the bot may pitch a genuinely new angle on this study as a fresh submission if one exists, but none was found here.
editor_notes.overall_assessment: REJECT. This is a duplicate of an article published minutes earlier from PR #2117, covering the same UC Berkeley/Nature Photonics computational-microscope study with the same figures, quotes, and sources, and offering no new information or angle. Independently, the submission also contains a fabricated Phys.org quote and a false claim that the Nature Photonics source was inaccessible when the snapshot shows it was fully readable (open access). Either issue alone would warrant scrutiny; together they clear the REJECT bar.
